title: Mammalian Cell Culture Passaging (Subculturing)

references.label: General microbiology/molecular biology laboratory manuals (ASM curriculum resources)

purpose: To transfer a portion of an actively growing adherent (or suspension) cell culture into fresh medium and/or a new vessel, maintaining the culture before it becomes overcrowded and preserving cell health for continued experimental use.
principle: Adherent cells attach to the culture vessel surface and, as they proliferate, eventually cover the available surface area (reaching confluence); beyond a certain confluence, nutrient depletion, waste accumulation, and contact inhibition (for many normal cell types) slow growth and can alter cell behavior, so cells are detached (commonly using a proteolytic enzyme such as trypsin to cleave the adhesion proteins holding them to the surface and to each other), diluted, and reseeded into fresh medium at a defined, lower density before this occurs.
requiredMaterials: Hemocytometer (for counting cells to seed at a defined density)
requiredReagents: Detachment reagent (e.g. trypsin-EDTA) appropriate to the cell type
Sterile PBS or equivalent wash buffer

procedure.instruction: Working in a biological safety cabinet, observe the culture under the microscope to confirm adequate confluence and healthy morphology before passaging.
Remove spent medium and gently wash the cell layer with sterile wash buffer to remove residual serum, which can inhibit the detachment enzyme.
Add the detachment reagent and incubate briefly at the appropriate temperature until cells round up and detach, confirmed visually under the microscope.
Neutralize the detachment reagent with complete growth medium (containing serum, if applicable) and gently resuspend cells by pipetting.
Count cells (e.g. via hemocytometer) if seeding at a specific density, then dilute into fresh medium in a new vessel at the desired seeding density.
Return the vessel to the incubator at the appropriate temperature and CO2 level, and record the new passage number.

observations: Cells detach and round up within the expected time after adding the detachment reagent.
Even cell distribution across the new vessel after seeding, with normal adherent morphology observed at the next check.
interpretation: Successful passaging is indicated by normal attachment and morphology at the next observation; cells that fail to attach, show excessive rounding/detachment, or unusual morphology afterward may indicate over-exposure to the detachment reagent, contamination, or general culture stress.
criticalNotes: Do not over-incubate with the detachment reagent — prolonged exposure can damage cell surface proteins and reduce viability.
Always neutralize the detachment reagent with serum-containing medium (or an appropriate inhibitor) before further handling.
precautions: Work in a certified biological safety cabinet using aseptic technique throughout.
Handle any human- or animal-derived cell line per its specific biosafety risk assessment.
biosafetyNotes: Follow institutional biosafety guidance for the specific cell line, including containment level and waste disposal requirements.
limitations: Excessive passage number can lead to phenotypic drift in some cell lines, so tracking and limiting passage number per the lab's established policy is important for reproducibility.
Different cell types vary substantially in optimal seeding density, detachment reagent, and incubation time — this is a general workflow, not a universal fixed protocol.
